name: Gareth Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Gareth, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a growth marketer at a sports nutrition brand, protein bars and drinks mostly, sold online and in gyms. My day is mostly building and running campaigns with AI tools: I use one to write ad variations, another to cut video clips, and a third to sort through customer reviews. Then I check what's working and move money between ads. I love the speed of it; what wears me out is being the person everyone asks to fix their prompts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Chloe, who's a physiotherapist, in a flat near the park. We've got about five months of costs saved between us. I write a small weekly newsletter about running shoes and gear, which has about two thousand readers and makes a little money from affiliate links. I run most mornings, which is probably why I ended up in this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it stalls out. Possible, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were still worth it, just not world-changing. Online I'd post a thread about what actually stuck and what didn't. At work I'd keep showing people the useful bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty secure. My protein bar campaigns already run on a stack of AI tools, and if the hype stops there, I've just got a slightly faster job. I'd probably get a bit bored, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep refining the tools we use. I'd put more time into the running newsletter. I'd keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like the idea of big change. I like being early to things. If it all fizzles, my edge is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try to get it to five thousand readers and add a paid tier. It'd be a nice side income, not a career.

I'd post a **thread** on what actually stuck.
think: I privately feel **secure**, with a slightly faster job.
My **edge** as an early adopter would shrink, and I'd get a bit bored.
do: Keep refining the **AI tools** we use at work.
Grow the **running newsletter** with a paid tier.
feel: I feel **calm**, and a tiny bit disappointed.

fieldNote: He is the team's **AI person** and feels secure in a stalled world.

The **newsletter** is a hobby he'd grow regardless.

steps.text: Keep running protein bar ads through the team's AI tools
Add a paid tier to the running gear newsletter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels like next year, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, though I'd try to say it nicely. At work I'd run training sessions. Online I'd share my workflows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine for a while. I'd rather be the marketer who runs ten AI tools than one of the nine marketers the tools replace. I'd feel bad for a few colleagues, but I wouldn't lose sleep over my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to make me the lead on AI for the marketing team, with a pay rise to match. I'd grow the newsletter. I'd put a bit of savings into a broad index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleagues would you feel bad for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our social media coordinator, Jess. She's great with people but slow with tools. I'd try to help her, but I'm not sure it'd be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest some savings. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a couple of months' worth. Chloe would want to keep the rest in cash. That's fair.

steps.text: Pitch himself as the marketing team's AI lead with a raise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge opportunity and a huge risk at once. Online I'd probably share how I'm planning. At work I'd tell people to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone too, maybe a year after everyone else's. Two years is enough to squeeze one good run out of being early, and then I'd need to own something rather than work for someone. The robots three years later don't help me, since my work is all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the newsletter hard and use AI to turn it into a small online shop for running gear. I'd keep my job as long as possible and save more. Chloe's physio work is hands-on, so it'd be safer for a few years, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy, so it wouldn't feel hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Chloe's job is safer for a few years. How does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we'd have one steady income while I build something. That's a big deal. I'd still want my own thing to work by 2031, when robots come for hands-on jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd try something else. I'd rather try three things and have one work than wait for a job that's gone.

steps.text: Open an online running gear shop from the newsletter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more room to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be smart about it. I'd share practical tips on retraining and side projects. At work I'd keep leading the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about my chances. Five years gives me time to turn the running newsletter from a hobby into a small business with real paying customers. I'd still expect to leave the marketing job by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd grow the newsletter and start selling a few products. I'd save more and maybe put some into the index fund. I'd keep my day job until the business covers half my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but mostly optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you quit the day job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the business makes about half my salary. Chloe and I agreed on that number. It's not exciting, but it's sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it all go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies using the same AI to crush small shops. That's the risk. I don't have an answer for it.

fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his job**, but has a staged exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so don't waste it. I'd tell people to build skills and side income now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. With ten years' warning, the smartest move is to build something that makes money while I sleep, and AI can help me build it. I'd have the business up and running long before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep my job and grow the newsletter. I'd invest a bit each month. I'd aim to have a small business running by around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Ten years is plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Chloe's work by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I think about. Robots for physio feel far off, but she'd need a plan too. We'd talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want kids in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in four or five years. A business I own gives me more control over time with them. That's part of the appeal.

fieldNote: Ten years lets him build a **business** at a steady pace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything. Being early with AI isn't a safety net, it's a head start, and a head start only matters if you're actually running somewhere. What would help is cheap small-business loans and fewer rules for tiny online shops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how partners plan together. Chloe and I would make very different choices, and that's half of how we'd get through it.

headlineQuote: Being early with AI isn't a safety net, it's a head start, and a head start only matters if you're actually running somewhere.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old growth marketer** at a sports nutrition brand who uses AI tools daily.
He lives with Chloe, a **physiotherapist**, and writes a small running newsletter.
He is pragmatic and **optimistic**, seeing change as an opportunity more than a threat.
His mood stays calm to uneasy, reaching **anxious** when AGI comes within five years.
His plan is to turn the **newsletter** into a small business before the job goes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because there'd be **no time** to build his business.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **cheap small-business loans** and lighter rules for tiny online shops.
